title: Package Namespace Architecture & Directory Structure
code:
# Visualizing the directory anatomy of a Python package:
"""
project/
│
├── main.py
│
└── tools/
    ├── __init__.py      <- Marks directory as a Python package
    ├── calculator.py    <- Submodule A
    └── string_utils.py  <- Submodule B
"""

# Simulated package object representation:
class ToolsPackage:
    class Calculator:
        @staticmethod
        def add(a, b):
            return a + b
        @staticmethod
        def multiply(a, b):
            return a * b

# Simulating 'from tools import calculator'
calculator = ToolsPackage.Calculator

print("Package demonstration:")
print("tools.calculator.add(10, 20)      =", calculator.add(10, 20))
print("tools.calculator.multiply(5, 6)   =", calculator.multiply(5, 6))
explanation: Illustrates how package directories act as parent namespaces grouping multiple submodules under a single logical folder.

title: Comparing Package Import Syntax Forms
code:
# Demonstrating the two primary styles of importing from a package:

# Style 1: Import module from package
# from tools import calculator
# Usage: calculator.add(15, 25)

# Style 2: Import specific function from package module
# from tools.calculator import add
# Usage: add(15, 25)

def simulate_imports():
    def add(x, y):
        return x + y
    
    print("Style 1 (from package import module)       : calculator.add(15, 25) ->", add(15, 25))
    print("Style 2 (from package.module import func) : add(15, 25)            ->", add(15, 25))

simulate_imports()
explanation: Compares importing a whole submodule versus importing individual functions directly from a package.

title: Multi-Module Package: Student Evaluation Suite
code:
# Simulating student_tools/ with marks.py and result.py

def calculate_total(marks):
    return sum(marks)

def calculate_average(marks):
    return sum(marks) / len(marks) if len(marks) > 0 else 0.0

def check_result(marks, pass_threshold=40):
    return "Pass" if all(m >= pass_threshold for m in marks) else "Fail"

# Sample student marks
scores = [85, 78, 92, 65, 88]
total = calculate_total(scores)
avg = calculate_average(scores)
status = check_result(scores)

print("===== STUDENT REPORT =====")
print("Scores  :", scores)
print("Total   :", total)
print("Average : %.2f" % avg)
print("Status  :", status)
explanation: Shows how dividing calculation and result evaluation into separate modules inside a student_tools package organizes real-world applications.

title: E-Commerce Billing Package Organization
code:
# Simulating billing/ package with calculation.py and invoice.py
def compute_subtotal(unit_price, quantity):
    return unit_price * quantity

def compute_discount(amount):
    return amount * 0.10 if amount >= 1000 else 0.0

def generate_invoice(item_name, price, qty):
    sub = compute_subtotal(price, qty)
    disc = compute_discount(sub)
    final = sub - disc
    return f"[INVOICE] {item_name} x {qty} | Subtotal: ${sub:.2f} | Discount: ${disc:.2f} | Final: ${final:.2f}"

print(generate_invoice("Mechanical Keyboard", 120.0, 10))
print(generate_invoice("USB-C Cable", 15.0, 2))
explanation: Demonstrates practical separation of concerns in a billing package where calculations feed into invoice generation.
